Former President of the Nigeria Scrabble Federation, Toke Aka, has urged President Bola Tinubu and the Federal Government to reward members of Team Nigeria following their impressive performance at the 16th African Scrabble Championship in Monrovia, Liberia. Aka said commendations alone were no longer enough, insisting that the players deserved tangible rewards and national recognition for their contributions to Nigeria’s sporting reputation. Nigeria’s 20-man contingent dominated the individual standings, won the Best Country award and recorded impressive results in the women’s category at the continental championship. Kogi State-born Abdulmumin Jimoh, who represents Ogun State, emerged individual champion with 23 victories and a cumulative spread of 1,760 points. His compatriot, George Ezinore of Edo State, finished second, while Emmanuel Umujose of Delta State completed an all-Nigerian podium. In the women’s category, 15-year-old Nigerian sensation Sophia Ekeruche finished second with 18 victories, behind Ghana’s Betty Kyeremateng, who claimed the Best Female Player award. Nigeria also won the Best Country title ahead of Kenya and hosts Liberia. For Aka, a former president of the Pan African Scrabble Association, the latest triumph is another chapter in Nigeria’s remarkable run of success in the sport, which he believes has not received commensurate government recognition. “These players deserve more than applause. They have worked extremely hard, sacrificed their time and resources, and competed against the best on the continent to bring honour and glory to Nigeria. “The Federal Government should see these achievements as a national asset. When our athletes go out there and conquer Africa and the world, the country must be ready to celebrate them, reward them and make them feel that their sacrifices are appreciated,” Aka said. He argued that rewarding sporting excellence would also encourage young Nigerians to pursue their talents and see sports as a viable career. “Rewarding these athletes sends a powerful message to the next generation that hard work pays. It tells a young Nigerian that if you dedicate yourself to excellence, represent your country with distinction and win laurels, your government will not turn its back on you. “That is how you build champions. You encourage those who are already performing, inspire upcoming talents and give parents confidence that sports can provide a meaningful future for their children,” he added. In 2024, Oluwatimilehin Doko won the 15th African Scrabble Championship in Kigali, Rwanda, becoming the youngest champion in the competition’s history at 24. Before him, Enoch Nwali claimed the continental title in Lusaka, Zambia, in 2022. However, Aka said the failure to fulfil promises made to some of the champions remained a concern. He recalled that Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu had promised to reward Nwali following his triumph in Zambia, but alleged that the commitment was never honoured. “Look at Enoch Nwali. He won the African championship in Lusaka and was promised a reward by the Lagos State Government. That promise was not fulfilled. What message are we sending to a young athlete who has worked so hard to become an African champion? “We cannot continue to encourage our athletes with promises that are never honoured. Government must understand that recognition must go beyond statements and congratulatory messages. There must be something tangible to show that the country values their achievements,” Aka said. He also cited Nigeria’s performance at the 2025 World Scrabble Championship in Accra, Ghana, where Team Nigeria defeated the United States to win the Best Country title, recording 350 wins and a cumulative spread of 8,975 points. Five Nigerians also finished among the world’s top 20 players, but Aka believes the achievement did not attract the national recognition that accompanies success in more popular sports. While former Presidents Olusegun Obasanjo and Goodluck Jonathan rewarded previous Nigerian Scrabble champions, the late President Muhammadu Buhari personally called Jighere to congratulate him following his world triumph. Aka said the gestures established a tradition that the current administration should sustain. “Previous administrations understood the importance of celebrating excellence in Scrabble. President Obasanjo and President Goodluck Jonathan rewarded champions, while President Muhammadu Buhari personally called Wellington Jighere when he made history in Australia. “These were important gestures. They showed that the Nigerian government was watching, that it appreciated the sacrifices of its sportsmen and women and that it was proud of their achievements. “We want this administration to do even better. President Tinubu should make these champions feel the pride of representing Nigeria. They deserve to be celebrated just like our footballers and basketball players,” he appealed. Nigeria’s success in Scrabble has also extended to the youth category, where its players have continued to win individual honours and major titles at continental and international competitions. The country’s young players delivered impressive performances at the African Youth Scrabble Championship in Kenya, following their exploits at the 2025 World Youth Scrabble Championship in Malaysia and the 2026 edition in Kenya. Aka believes rewarding the senior champions and recognising emerging talents would help sustain Nigeria’s dominance in the sport. “These children are the future of Nigerian Scrabble. They are winning titles against the best young players in the world, and they deserve encouragement. “When government rewards these young champions, it motivates them to remain committed to the sport. It also encourages other children to discover their talents and understand that they too can achieve something remarkable for their country. “Scrabble is not just a game. It develops intelligence, vocabulary, concentration, strategic thinking and mental discipline. These are qualities our education system and society should encourage,” he said. Aka’s appeal comes amid concerns over the disparity in government recognition of sporting achievements in Nigeria, with footballers and basketball teams often attracting more public attention and rewards than athletes in less commercially popular sports. Although the National Sports Commission has acknowledged Nigeria’s latest continental triumph by receiving the victorious team and expressing its commitment to developing the sport, Aka believes the government must go further by introducing tangible rewards for the players. He urged Tinubu, the NSC, the Federal Ministry of Education and other relevant government institutions to work together to honour the champions. “These are national heroes and heroines. They have done what many people only dream of doing. They have carried Nigeria’s flag across Africa and the world and returned with victories that have brought pride to millions of Nigerians. “We are not asking government to do anything extraordinary. We are asking it to recognise excellence, honour commitment and reward those who have brought glory to this country. “Let the Federal Government host these champions, celebrate them publicly and give them the rewards they deserve. Let their achievements be documented and used to inspire the next generation. “These players work day and night to remain competitive. They deserve to know that their country stands behind them. Nigeria must not wait until these champions retire before appreciating what they have done,” Aka concluded.
